opus-5.5.text:
I think openness was really the engine of the field during that period. If you look at how deep learning progressed from roughly 2012 to 2020, it was a very collaborative effort across labs, both academic and industrial. People published their papers, they released their code, and very often they released their models and weights as well. That meant that when one group had a good idea, say a new normalization technique, a better optimizer, or the attention mechanism, everybody else could pick it up within weeks, reproduce it, and build on top of it.

That made the whole field move much faster than any single organization could have on its own. You had this compounding effect: Google would publish something, Meta would improve on it, a university lab would find a flaw or a simplification, and then it would go back into the common pool of knowledge. The transformer itself is a good example. It was published openly, and the entire ecosystem, including the work that eventually led to large language models, came out of people being able to take that architecture and iterate on it freely.

I was at DeepMind during part of that time, and before that in academia, and the culture was very much about sharing. Conferences like NeurIPS and ICML were where everything happened, and there was a strong norm that if you didn't release enough detail to reproduce your results, the work was considered less credible.

What changed around 2020 is that some of the leading labs started to close up, partly for competitive reasons and partly with safety arguments. I think that was a bit of a pity, because it slowed down the circulation of ideas. Part of the reason we started Mistral was the conviction that this open approach, releasing strong models with open weights, is still the best way to make progress, to let the community scrutinize the technology, and to make sure that it isn't controlled by just a handful of companies.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers published papers, code, and models, allowing other groups to reproduce and build on ideas, and credits this open collaboration with accelerating progress before 2020.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think if you look at the history of the field, essentially everything that got us to where we are was built in the open. The research culture was academic in nature: you published at NeurIPS or ICML, you put your code on GitHub, you released your weights, and the next lab built on top of you within weeks. The transformer paper itself, word2vec, ResNets, the attention mechanisms, the optimizers we all use, PyTorch and TensorFlow as frameworks, the ImageNet dataset, all of this was shared freely. And that's precisely why the pace was so fast. You had thousands of people across the world iterating on the same ideas in parallel, correcting each other's mistakes, and reproducing results. Progress compounded because nobody had to re-derive things behind closed doors.

What's interesting is that this was true even for the industrial labs. When I was at DeepMind, the expectation was still that you would publish, and Google Brain and FAIR were the same. The competitive dynamic was about talent and reputation, and reputation came from putting things out. So openness wasn't a charitable act, it was the operating system of the field, and the companies benefited from it as much as academia did.

I'd say two things changed around 2020. The first is that scale started to matter in a way that made the artifacts themselves, the trained models, enormously expensive, and so the weights became something you could decide to withhold. GPT-3 was really the moment where a frontier lab chose to publish a paper describing the result but not release the model. The second is that the technology became commercially relevant enough that the incentives shifted toward secrecy. And so you went in a few years from a field where everything was reproducible to one where the most important results could not be verified by anyone outside a handful of companies.

My view is that this is a loss, and not only on principle. When you close things, you lose the error correction, you lose the long tail of people finding new use cases, you concentrate the understanding of how these systems work in very few hands. That's bad for science and I also think it's bad for safety, because you can't audit what you can't see. So part of what we are trying to do at Mistral is to show that the frontier doesn't have to be closed, that you can build a real business while keeping the weights available, and in doing so keep the field in the mode that made it productive in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says the field’s work was shared openly, allowing labs to build on one another’s work within weeks, and directly credits that exchange with the fast pace of progress.

astra-6.text:
I think openness was really central to that progress. Researchers would publish their results, share code, and often release models, so other teams could reproduce the work and build on it. You didn’t have to rediscover everything yourself before you could contribute something new.

And that created a very fast feedback loop between academia and industry. A technique developed in one lab could be tested, challenged, and improved by many others. So I think it’s difficult to separate the speed of progress in machine learning during that period from the culture of sharing that supported it.

r001.rationale: The response links rapid pre-2020 progress to sharing results, code, and models, which let other teams reproduce and build on work from other labs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think openness was fundamental. Before 2020, machine learning progressed through a very collaborative research culture. People published their methods, shared code, and often released models, so other teams could reproduce the results and build on them. You didn’t have to rediscover everything yourself before you could contribute something new.

That made the feedback loop very fast. An idea could come from one lab, get tested and improved somewhere else, and become a standard tool across the field. So I see openness as a big part of the explanation for that progress: it allowed knowledge to accumulate across institutions, rather than staying within individual organizations.

r001.rationale: The response links pre-2020 progress to shared methods, code, and models that let other teams reproduce and improve on work from other labs.
